title: Containers cut the cost of loading a ship from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents

cover.alt: The container ship NYK Virgo at sea, its deck stacked high with coloured shipping containers.

body: Before 1956, cargo went aboard ship piece by piece: gangs of 20 to 22 longshoremen packed sacks, crates and barrels into the hold, and hand-loading cost about **$5.86 a ton**. Trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean knew that a ship earns money only at sea, and on 26 April 1956 his converted tanker *Ideal X* sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston carrying 58 trailer-sized boxes that cranes could lift straight off trucks. Loading by container cost about **16 cents a ton**, a 36-fold saving, and sealed boxes also cut the theft that had long plagued the docks. Standard sizes agreed through ISO between 1968 and 1970 let any crane, ship, train or truck handle any box, and by 2009 about 90% of the world's non-bulk cargo travelled in containers. When McLean died in 2001, container ships around the world blew their whistles on the morning of his funeral.

slides.question: Hand-loading cost $5.86 a ton. In cents, what did loading a ton by container cost?
slides.explanation: About 16 cents a ton, a 36-fold saving. A crane lifted a whole box at once instead of dozens of hands moving every sack and crate.

slides.question: What did the Ideal X carry on 26 April 1956?
options: A cargo of oil, its original job
slides.explanation: The refitted tanker carried 58 trailer vans, 35 feet long, later simply called containers. Standard 20- and 40-foot sizes came with the ISO rules of 1968 to 1970.
